summary: Last Contact is an interactive website that tells the stories of eight machines NASA left on the Moon and Mars, made for school-age and casual space fans. The home page is a spider web with Earth at the centre, and each machine is a node: Surveyor 3, Apollo 11 Eagle, Apollo 12 Intrepid, Apollo 15 Falcon, Mars Pathfinder, Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity. Tapping one opens a story page where the machine speaks in the first person and its final message types out. Real mission facts, NASA photos, an animation and a short quiz explain what it was built to do and what it discovered. A signal timeline shows each machine’s last contact date. A rover distance race ends with Perseverance passing Opportunity’s record on October 11, 2026. The project turns dense mission data into a story, so young explorers feel a personal connection to hardware that is no longer in the news.
details:
What it does: Visitors explore a web of eight retired NASA machines. Each story page has a first-person “last transmission”, fact cards, a NASA photo, and a one-question quiz. Surveyor 3 has an interactive two-bounce landing animation. Pathfinder has an airbag-bounce animation. The Spirit and Opportunity page has a rover distance race. A timeline page shows every machine’s last contact date.

Why it matters: Young people mostly hear about active missions. This shows how the engineering of old hardware led to real discoveries, such as Surveyor 3 proving the Moon’s soil could hold an Apollo lander, and Spirit and Opportunity showing that water once lasted on Mars.

Tools: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, SVG and canvas animation, hosted as a single web page. Fonts: Fraunces, Atkinson Hyperlegible and IBM Plex Mono. NASA photos were cropped and sharpened.

Creativity: The “last contact” idea, with each machine speaking in its own voice, and the web layout with Earth as the hub.

Accessibility and accuracy: It respects reduced-motion settings, shows keyboard focus, has labelled images, works on phones, and uses high-contrast colours. All facts come from the NASA pages listed in the resources. Apollo 12’s landing is given as November 19 in Universal Time and November 18 in US time.

SI use: The code, text and illustrations were created with help from Claude, an AI assistant from Anthropic. The team reviewed and edited them. The NASA photographs are real and are credited to NASA.
